extracted.intended_audience: scientists and scientifically literate readers (Nature readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing short scientific letters, notes and correspondence (observational reports, brief theoretical proposals, critiques) for a multidisciplinary scientific journal. Emphasises concise methods, evidence, and practical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require experimental confirmation for theoretical conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions arrived at are purely theoretical, and have at present no experimental confirmation; the practical test outlined at the end of the paper should supply a definite answer as to whether there is any foundation for the theory advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists should explicitly state that claims lack experimental confirmation and propose concrete, practicable tests that would provide a definitive check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose measurable, operational methods
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hoped to show a means whereby [gyro-viscosity] may be measured. A method of doing this which suggests itself is based upon the correct resolution of the forces which go to produce the so-called Couette correction for flow through capillary tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing a new concept or phenomenon, outline specific measurement approaches and tie them to existing measurable corrections or empirical quantities (e.g., Couette correction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about limits of current understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: While our ideas are in their present state of flux, we cannot be sufficiently definite about anything in this connexion to attempt any sort of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate what can be rigorously analysed from conjecture; avoid presenting tentative ideas as established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer components amenable to mathematical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas (a) [gyro-viscosity] lends itself readily to mathematical treatment, (b) [molecular friction or deformation] is still so largely a matter of conjecture that ... we cannot be sufficiently definite ... to attempt any sort of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When decomposing a phenomenon, identify and prioritise parts that allow quantitative/mathematical analysis and state explicitly which parts remain qualitative or speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement precision must be sufficient to resolve effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial momentary resistance should be greater than the subsequent constant resistance; and since the former is independent of the rate ... it would afford a means of estimating the relative molecular gyro-viscosity, if only it could be measured with sufficient accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether available instrumentation and methods can achieve the accuracy required to detect the predicted effect before claiming feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough mathematical and mechanistic modelling of flow fields
rubrics_metrics.description: We are faced with the problem of finding (1) an expression for the distribution of the velocities in the trumpet-shaped lines of flow of the liquid before it enters the tube; (2) the varying acceleration ...; (3) the influence of the head of liquid on the curvature of these lines. As all of these admit of exact mathematical treatment, it should be possible ... to calculate Wc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, break complex fluid/mechanical problems into mathematically tractable subproblems and indicate how model outputs connect to measurable quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experimental procedure and timings precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: At 11.30 A.M., September 22, the crabs, carrying altogether 18 anemones, were fed with cockles and queens. At 12.5 P.M. all anemones were open ... On September 29 the experiment was repeated ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise timestamps, sample counts and procedural details for observational experiments to allow reproducibility and clear interpretation of behaviour changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use replication and repeated trials
rubrics_metrics.description: The experiment was repeated ... All the anemones soon put their discs flat on the ground, and those which were sitting horizontally bobbed their discs down on the ground within a few minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat experiments under similar conditions to assess consistency of responses; report repetitions and whether results were concordant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for and acknowledge confounding variables
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not possible to see whether the unusual movements of the crabs on the addition of food, or the smell of the added food, caused the anemones to react as they did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify plausible alternative causes for observed effects, acknowledge inability to isolate causes when relevant, and, when possible, design experiments to disambiguate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer observations in naturalistic as well as controlled conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In most figures ... the anemone is shown with its tentacles beautifully expanded ... When these hermit-crabs with their associated anemones are caught fresh in the trawl it may be observed that although the anemones come up closed in no case are they sitting on the shell as is shown in the well-known figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare textbook/illustrative depictions with fresh field observations; report discrepancies and consider ecological/contextual behaviour when interpreting laboratory results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe sample acquisition and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of fresh hermit-crabs and anemones was obtained by trawling in September 1920 and a few experiments made in a tank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how specimens/samples were obtained (method, date, location) so readers can assess representativeness and potential collection biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive, evidence-based criticism in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Helpful criticism is welcome to an author, and the correction of errors can be the making of a second edition of a text-book; but adverse criticism in which personal bias of opinion is allowed to outweigh generally accepted beliefs can have little value either for the author or for the reading public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should aim to correct errors and improve work, avoiding personal bias; criticisms should be based on evidence and reasoned argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite authority and evidence when criticising
rubrics_metrics.description: I beg him to accept my assurance that it was solely to my regard for space in your columns that any such bluntness was due. It was from like considerations that I was obliged to refrain from indicating the authority for and adducing evidence in support of some of my criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where space allows, reviewers should indicate authorities and present evidence supporting critiques; lack of citation weakens critical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design pedagogical material with practical constraints in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: I agree that it is desirable to introduce plant physiology at an earlier stage in the course; but, with the exception of germination (which is introduced in the Easter Term), the experiments seldom yield good results in the winter months. The school year begins towards the end of September, and the arrangement of the chapters (as stated in the preface) was based upon this assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks and course materials should account for local schedules, seasonality and resource constraints so experimental exercises are feasible and yield reliable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations of experimental apparatus and avoid overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical difficulty of setting up a series of short threads, evenly spaced, evenly graduated in tension, and maintaining their spacing and tension unaltered during and after the processes of fixation, embedding and immersion in fluid, is so great that I have not succeeded so far in attaining anything approaching accuracy. One need scarcely say that so imperfect an apparatus cannot, in its present state, throw much light on the more recondite points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report technical limitations of apparatus and restrict claims to what the apparatus can reasonably resolve; identify which phenomena are beyond current setup's resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and test critical assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If I understand Dr. Perrett’s letter ... his objection ... is based on the assumption that the intensity of the stimulation of every part of the cochlea must be proportional to the amplitude of the vibration set up in that part. I think this assumption is unwarranted ... the intensity of the sensory impression may vary also with the rapidity and the rate of change of direction of the movement ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state key assumptions underlying interpretations; discuss alternative formulations and, where possible, propose tests to distinguish them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proposing clinical/therapeutic procedures, use empirically validated compatibility testing
rubrics_metrics.description: It was soon found that the capacity of the body to identify any blood as foreign ... If from a dozen people a few cubic centimetres of blood are withdrawn ... mixed with a little of each serum ... it will be found that the results are not all the same ... serious trouble may be caused [by agglutination]. It is therefore not every human blood that is suitable for transfusion into a given person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before transfusion or equivalent biological interventions, perform in vitro compatibility tests (serum/corpuscle mixing) and only proceed when compatibilities are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply and report established classification rules for compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: By sorting over a large number of people by this test it has been found that they may be classified into four groups ... The blood characteristics of the four groups are: Group I. [neither serum agglutinates] ... Group IV. [a and b present in serum] ... The corpuscles of Group I. can safely be put only into recipients belonging to the same group ... those of Group IV. into anybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the established group classifications (A/B, a/b factors) to guide transfusion decisions; explicitly state donor and recipient group memberships and allowed matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical effects of plasma dilution and reagent differences
rubrics_metrics.description: When, for example, Group IV. blood is transfused, the plasma of it should agglutinate the corpuscles of the recipient if the reaction took place as it does outside the body. This does not appear to happen, or if it does it produces no obvious ill-effects ... It is most probably due to the quantity of transfused plasma being insufficient, when diluted with the recipient’s blood, to cause a significant agglutination ... The fact that it is plasma which is injected and not serum may also have some influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for in vivo dilution effects and the biochemical differences between plasma and serum when extrapolating in vitro compatibility results to clinical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blood-group inheritance knowledge cautiously for forensic/parentage testing
rubrics_metrics.description: In inheritance these qualities have been shown to be transmitted as straightforward Mendelian factors. It follows that the blood of parents and children are by no means necessarily compatible ... The possibility of using these blood reactions to investigate cases of disputed parentage has been carefully worked out ... the method can have but a limited application, though the answers are conclusive if they can be obtained at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply blood-group incompatibility as one line of evidence in parentage disputes but be aware of its limited discriminatory power and present limitations clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider population frequencies and racial/ethnic variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of much interest also is the observation that the proportion of the population falling into Groups II. and III. varies a good deal in different races. In England about 40 per cent. are Group II., about 15 per cent. Group III., Groups I. and IV. giving about 2[5?].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying classification-based rules (medical, forensic, demographic), report and consider local population frequencies and their variation across groups or races.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proposing systemic reforms, weigh practical adoption costs and social acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: If it were a case of starting with a clean sheet there would be no greater difficulty in adopting the metric system ... The British yard has become very widely known, whereas the metre is quite unknown ... It has taken fifty years to spread the knowledge of the 80-tola seer to the extent now achieved; to introduce a new unit would mean starting all over again ... Interference of such a kind as would be required to enforce the use of a new system of weights and measures means interference by a large and therefore necessarily low-paid staff ... We found a very general desire for a uniform system of weights and measures, but for one based on a unit that was known, and hence we recommended that system which could be adopted with very much less difficulty than any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy proposals (e.g., standardisation) should account for entrenched local units, administrative costs, public education burdens, and cultural resistance; prefer transitions that minimise disruption while achieving sufficient standardisation benefits.
